title: Credential split in text but rebuilt by the language that reads it
description: A credential is written across a line break or across several string pieces in a carrier whose language rebuilds the original value before the program uses it: a shell backslash-newline, a string-literal line continuation, or concatenated string literals.
semantics: The language removes the separator or concatenates the pieces, so the value the program sees is the intact credential. Every fragment of the value is covered; the separators (backslash, line break, quotes, operator) are not part of it. This holds per mechanism, and only for a mechanism a cited language definition states: it never licenses removing whitespace in general.

applicability.rationale: Carrier-level: the reasoning is about the language construct, not about a credential family.

evidenceBasis.rationale: Each mechanism is stated by two language definitions from different maintainers (shell: POSIX and the GNU Bash manual; string-literal continuation and concatenation: the Python reference and ECMAScript). The record claims consistency of those texts with the reading, not a provider rule. Whether a given carrier is read by such a language at all is per fixture and per Case.

sources.supports: If a newline follows the backslash, the shell shall interpret this as line continuation; the backslash and newline are removed before splitting the input into tokens.
An unquoted backslash-newline pair is treated as a line continuation: removed from the input stream and effectively ignored.
A backslash followed by a newline inside a string literal is an ignored end of line: neither is part of the string value.
A LineContinuation in a string literal has the empty String as its string value, and a line terminator can appear in a string literal only as part of one.

notes: Project-authored by the Redact Secret project, which maintains this repository; not independent evidence. Draft; not yet reviewed.
